title: A minister is offered deliverance if he will be baptized
setting: On 5 January 1831, three days after the Church conference, Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Fayette, New York. It was for a minister named James, who had covenanted to obey any command given through Joseph. Later printings name him James Covel or Covill. The Joseph Smith Papers favor James Covel, a Methodist elder near Canandaigua, but no source settles his identity.
summary: The voice speaks as Jesus Christ, who gives power to become his sons to all who receive him. It defines the gospel as repentance, baptism by water, and then the baptism of fire and the Holy Ghost. It tells James that his heart is right at this time. It also says he has rejected the Lord many times because of pride and worldly cares. If he will arise and be baptized, it promises a blessing greater than he has known. It calls him to preach, but in the Ohio, not in the eastern countries. It says the Ohio people pray in faith, and judgment will be stayed only if they repent. James is to baptize and lay on hands for the gift of the Holy Ghost.

contextNote.title: Why James had seen great sorrow
contextNote.text: James came with a sincere promise, yet the revelation looks back on a troubled past. Verse 8 says his heart is “right before me at this time”. Verse 9 explains his sorrow: he had rejected the Lord “many times because of pride and the cares of the world”. Verse 10 answers that pattern with an opening: “the days of thy deliverance are come”. The condition is plain, since he must arise and be baptized. In this passage, sorrow is the result of repeated refusal, and deliverance depends on acting now.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 37–40 points to James Covel’s story when teaching that eternal riches outweigh earthly ones. What does the phrase “at this time” in verse 8 suggest about why verse 10 urges him to act now?
reviewNote: Read all 24 verses. Official heading gives Fayette, 5 January 1831, to James Covel, a former Methodist minister, who had covenanted to obey. JSP notes the earliest copy says only “James”; identity rests on later printings, and JSP favors a Methodist James Covel near Canandaigua over Baptist James Covill. Kirtland stands in for “the Ohio”. Fact-check 2026-10-12: no changes. Setting checked against the official heading and JSP historical introduction.
